summary: Specifies Manufacturer Usage Descriptions, an architecture that lets end devices signal to the network what access and functionality they need. The initial focus is access control.

eli5.summary: A toy comes with a note saying it only needs to talk to these places. The network can then block everything else.

questions: how does mud url work with dhcp
subtitle: How a device can point the network to a signed file saying what traffic it is meant to send and receive.

tldr.problem: Devices built for one narrow purpose, such as a light bulb, only need a few communication patterns, but networks have no standard way to learn what those are and block everything else.
tldr.mechanism: The device emits a MUD URL (by DHCP, an X.509 certificate extension or LLDP). A MUD manager fetches the signed MUD file from that https URL, a YANG-based JSON access list, and turns it into local network configuration.
tldr.outcome: MUD gives a way to scale access policy across many device types, but the file is a suggestion that the local administrator can ignore, and it does not replace patching.

facts.label: cache-validity limit
facts.value: At most 168 hours; at least 24 recommended

today: RFC 8520 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the access list model of RFC 8519.

sections.title: The Idea Behind MUD
sections.content:
General purpose computers can decide for themselves what to do. The RFC focuses on Things: devices that are specifically not meant for general purpose computing and so have a small number of communication patterns. Those patterns can be written down as a Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) and applied at various points in a network. MUD mainly addresses threats to the device, rather than the device as a threat.

"Manufacturer" is used loosely: it is the organization in the supply chain that takes responsibility for telling the network what the device is for. The RFC lists the goals: reduce the threat surface to the intended communications, scale network policy to growing numbers of device types, mitigate some vulnerabilities faster than updates can be made (especially for unsupported systems), keep implementation cost low, and allow extensibility.

It also says what MUD does not do. It is not for general purpose computers, it never replaces the need for manufacturers to patch vulnerabilities, and a MUD file contains suggestions, not directives. The local network administrator decides what is appropriate.
sections.eli5: A light bulb only needs to talk to its app, so a note on the box saying "only let me talk to my app" lets the house block everyone else from poking it.

sections.title: The Architecture and Order of Operations
sections.content:
MUD has three building blocks: a URL that locates a description, the description itself, and a way for local network management to retrieve it. Four roles appear. The Thing emits the MUD URL. A switch or router collects it. The MUD manager, a network management system that may be part of an AAA system, receives it and fetches the MUD file from a MUD file server, typically run by or for the manufacturer. For legacy devices that cannot emit a URL, a switch may supply one, for example hardcoded on a port or mapped from an L2 address or certificate hash.

The RFC gives one intended order. The Thing emits a URL and the nearest switch forwards it. The manager retrieves the file and signature unless it already has copies, validates the signature, and may check reputation services. It may ask the administrator for permission, then instantiates local configuration from the abstractions, configures the nearest switch, and removes the policy when the Thing disconnects.

MUD URLs MUST use the https scheme. Managers SHOULD fetch with GET, MUST validate the server certificate, and SHOULD send an Accept header containing application/mud+json. If a fetch fails, the manager SHOULD consider the existing file safe to use for a while and log the failure after some period.
sections.eli5: The toy shows its note to the doorman. The doorman calls the office, the office gets the full rules from the toy maker, checks they are real, and tells the doorman which doors the toy may use.

sections.title: The MUD File and Its Classes
sections.content:
A MUD file is a YANG model instance serialized as JSON. It is limited to three schemas: ietf-access-control-list from RFC 8519, plus ietf-mud and ietf-acldns from this RFC. A valid file has two root objects, a mud container and an acls container. The mud container carries metadata such as mud-version (this memo specifies version 1), mud-url, last-update, mud-signature, is-supported and systeminfo. It also holds from-device-policy and to-device-policy, which refer to access lists for each direction of traffic.

The cache-validity value is in hours. It is RECOMMENDED to be no less than 24, and it MUST NOT be more than 168 for any supported Thing.

To avoid hard-coded addresses, the model adds abstractions that the local deployment turns into real addresses. manufacturer and same-manufacturer match the authority part of another Thing's MUD URL. controller and my-controller refer to hosts the administrator has registered as controllers. local-networks means hosts within the local administrative boundary, by default the local subnet. There is also direction-initiated for TCP, so that traffic toward a Thing is dropped unless the Thing started the connection. Publishers SHOULD use these abstractions and avoid IP addresses, and a manager SHOULD NOT automatically implement a file containing IP addresses.

The ietf-acldns module adds src-dnsname and dst-dnsname, so a cloud service can be named by domain name. A MUD file MUST NOT use src-dnsname in from-device-policy or dst-dnsname in to-device-policy.

By default, anything not explicitly permitted is denied, and local DNS and NTP are permitted to and from the Thing. These defaults apply after all explicit rules, so an explicit drop can change them. Only accept and drop actions SHOULD be used, and managers MAY ignore any part of a description or all of it.
sections.eli5: The note uses words like "my maker's other gadgets" and "things in this house" instead of street addresses, because the toy maker does not know where you live. Your house fills in the real addresses.

sections.title: Three Ways to Emit the MUD URL
sections.content:
The RFC defines three means for a Thing to announce its MUD URL, and notes that other means are possible.

DHCP. The IPv4 option has code OPTION_MUD_URL_V4 (161) and a length byte, followed by a MUD string. The IPv6 option is OPTION_MUD_URL_V6 (112). The whole option MUST NOT exceed 255 octets. A client may emit at most one MUD URL option per IP version, and if both are sent the same URL MUST be used. A DHCP server may ignore the option, forward it to a MUD manager, or fetch the file itself. There are no additional requirements for relays.

X.509. A non-critical certificate extension holds a single URL for the certificate subject, which fits IEEE 802.1AR device certificates. A separate extension, id-pe-mudsigner, holds the subject of the certificate that signs the MUD file.

LLDP. A vendor-specific TLV (type 127) with the IANA organizationally unique identifier 00 00 5E and subtype 1 carries the MUD string, up to 255 octets. LLDP is one-way, nothing is acknowledged, and no specific network behavior is guaranteed.
sections.eli5: The toy can show its note in three ways: say it out loud when it joins the network, carry it on an ID card, or hold up a sign to its neighbor.

sections.title: Signed MUD Files
sections.content:
Because MUD files can configure access lists, they are sensitive. A MUD file MUST be signed using DER-encoded Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) as an opaque binary object, and the signature is transferred with content type application/pkcs7-signature. Intermediate certificates SHOULD be included, and the signature is found through the mud-signature value in the file.

Before processing the rest of a file, the MUD manager MUST retrieve the signature and validate it across the file. The signing certificate MUST have the digitalSignature(0) key usage bit set. If the device's certificate has an id-pe-mudsigner extension, the signing certificate's subject MUST match it. If these checks fail, or the chain of trust to a known trust anchor cannot be validated, the manager MUST stop processing until an administrator approves.

The signature assigns accountability to an entity whose reputation can guide administrators. The signer is likely the manufacturer but does not have to be, for example when integrators install their own certificates.
sections.eli5: The note has a signature, like a teacher signing a permission slip. If the signature does not check out, nobody follows the note until a grown-up says it is okay.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If the MUD URL is sent by DHCP or LLDP, a Thing may lie about what it is and gain extra access, for example by being admitted to same-manufacturer or my-controller. Implementations SHOULD be configurable to disallow additive access for URLs not emitted in a secure fashion, such as in a certificate. Devices may also forge L2 or L3 source information, so deployments should bind communications to the authentication, for example with MACsec for 802.1X.

A rogue certification authority could sign a certificate with the same subject as the MUDsigner field. The manager can flag a changed signer, SHOULD seek administrator approval if the file also changes, and MUST keep a cache of trusted CAs. If a domain changes ownership, the new owner could serve MUD files that managers accept, so managers SHOULD cache the file server's certificates and look for ownership changes.

There are privacy concerns too. Releasing a MUD URL reveals what the Thing is, which guides an attacker toward likely vulnerabilities, and it may help an observer identify individuals when combined with other information. The RFC suggests data minimization and mechanisms such as TEAP and DHCPv6-Shield, and notes that a MUD manager could itself be spied on.
sections.eli5: A sneaky toy could claim to be a different kind of toy to get more freedom, so the house should trust notes that come on a proper ID card more than ones the toy just shouts out.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Policy can be enforced on the nearest switch or access point to protect a Thing from other Things nearby, or as close to the Internet as possible to limit unwanted traffic. If enforcement is not available at the closest hop, the risk of lateral infection between nearby devices grows.

Adding a Thing to the manufacturer or same-manufacturer class can grow the access lists on switches connected to other Things, so the growth needs managing, and network segmentation can help.

The RFC expects many devices not to support MUD yet. Whether a newly connected device gets broad or limited access is a local decision, and a deployment may ignore a MUD policy entirely and use the MUD URL only as a classifier in its own policy.

Extensions are tightly limited. Only additions to the mud container that add no risk to the Thing are allowed. They SHALL be standardized through the IETF process, MUST be named in the extensions list, and managers MUST ignore nodes they do not understand.
sections.eli5: You can put the guard at the toy's own door or at the front gate of the house. Each choice protects against different problems, and the house owner decides.

viz.caption: MATCH ABSTRACTIONS IN THE MUD MODEL

items.label: Manufacturer
items.desc: Devices whose MUD URL authority matches a named host.

items.label: Same manufacturer
items.desc: Devices with the same MUD URL authority as this Thing.

items.label: Controller
items.desc: Hosts the local administrator has registered for a named class.

items.label: My controller
items.desc: Hosts mapped to this MUD URL by the manager.

items.label: Local networks
items.desc: Addresses within the local administrative boundary, by default the local subnet.
